title: Discovering Phase Space Structure in Learned Hamiltonian Systems
claim: A single shared latent dynamics backbone maps random samples through a structured physical model to generate multiple observation modalities.
layout: 3 panels: top backbone flows left-to-right, two decoder branches below
description: A wide figure with a peach rounded box on top and two green rounded boxes below. In the top box, data flows left to right. A Gaussian bell curve labelled Motion Sample gives a point epsilon_m. That point passes through a box f, the Phase Space Map, which also takes a system-info node xi. The output is a point z_0 on a curved grid surface. z_0, a second xi node and a control input u all feed a dashed Port-Hamiltonian Neural Network box. Inside it, a trapezoid H leads to the partial derivatives dH/dq and dH/dp. These produce the red-outlined Phase Space Rollout z_1..z_T. Below, panel (a) takes z_0:T through a trapezoid Trajectory Generator G_T to a plot of curves. Panel (b) takes z_0:T and epsilon_c through an Image Generator G_I to a stack of video frames with coloured dots.
caption: SPS-GAN generates trajectories and videos across multiple systems through a shared phase-space backbone. Random motion samples ϵm and system information ξ are passed through the phase-space map f to produce an initial phase-space state z0. This state is evolved forward in time by a Port-Hamiltonian Neural Network [15] conditioned on ξ, yielding the phase-space trajectory [z0:T ], which is decoded to (a) Cartesian trajectory [ˆx0:T ] and (b) video frames [ˆv0:T ].
abstract: Mechanics-inspired neural networks provide physically structured models of dynamical systems, but typically assume access to the coordinates in which the underlying dynamics are expressed. While recent generative approaches relax this assumption, they remain limited in their ability to jointly model different dynamical regimes and discover interpretable latent structure. We introduce Structured Phase Space GAN (SPS-GAN), a conditional generative framework that learns mechanical dynamics and discovers latent phase-space structure from Cartesian trajectories or video observations. We achieve this by combining adversarial generation with port-Hamiltonian latent dynamics and extending cyclic-coordinate regularization to account for dissipation and forcing. This formulation supports conservative, dissipative, and forced systems while encouraging compact latent representations from which active degrees of freedom can be identified. Experiments on simulated and real-world systems demonstrate improved trajectory accuracy and video generation quality over competitive baselines, while identifying active latent dimensions consistent with the expected effective degrees of freedom and recovering physically interpretable coordinates across observation modalities and dynamical regimes.
